The Red Hills salamander Phaeognathus hubrichti is a large, secretive plethodontid endemic to a narrow region of southern Alabama. Field surveys over several decades have documented that newly hatched individuals emerge from their subterranean nests following an incubation period of approximately 80 days [ab = approximately 80 days] when the surrounding substrate temperature is consistently near 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a thermal regime typical of the deep burrows this species inhabits. At this critical hatching event, the wet weight at birth is remarkably low, averaging just 0.179 grams [Wwb = 0.179 grams], a value derived from the species’ unusually large but yolk-rich eggs which measure about 7 millimeters in diameter. This modest neonatal mass underscores the extreme lecithotrophy of the hatchlings, which depend entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during their first weeks of life. Following eclosion from the gelatinous egg capsule, the endotrophic larva undergoes a rapid phase of yolk absorption before transitioning to a free-living existence within the moist, sandy loam soils of the steep ravines that characterize its habitat.

As the juvenile salamander matures, it undergoes a pronounced allometric shift during the larval-juvenile transition, culminating in metamorphosis. The snout-vent length at metamorphosis, based on extensive museum collections and mark-recapture studies, is approximately 3.7 centimeters , representing a threshold size that must be attained before the gill-breathing larva can complete tail resorption and skin keratinisation for terrestrial life. At a stable burrow temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a thermal condition common in the deeper chambers where these animals shelter, the time since birth at sexual maturity has been estimated at 5 years [tp = 5 years], a remarkably protracted developmental delay for a plethodontid salamander. This extended period of somatic growth reflects the species’ low metabolic rate and the challenges of foraging for invertebrate prey in a resource-poor subterranean environment. Only after this 5-year period do the gonads begin to mature, with males typically showing signs of gametogenesis onset and females initiating vitellogenesis.

Reproductive output in Phaeognathus hubrichti is exceptionally low, consistent with its K-selected life history strategy. Females produce clutches of approximately 7 eggs [N_R_i = clutches of approximately 7 eggs] and, under the cool conditions prevalent in their burrows at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], they typically deposit only a single clutch every other year [F_R_i = single clutch every other year]. This means that an adult female may produce, on average, just one clutch over a 2-year period, a rate that is among the lowest documented for any North American salamander. The size of the eggs is substantial, which explains the relatively large hatchling mass despite the low fecundity. This conservative reproductive strategy is likely an adaptation to the stable but unproductive conditions of the deep-soil environment, where predation on eggs and larvae is minimal but food availability for growing juveniles is limiting.

Adult body size in this species shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with males attaining a significantly greater ultimate wet weight than females. Records from long-term field studies indicate that the ultimate wet weight for females rarely exceeds 14 grams [Wwi = 14 grams], a figure that reflects the energetic constraints of egg production and the associated high investment per offspring. In contrast, males commonly achieve an ultimate wet weight of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams], a size advantage that likely enhances their competitive ability during the breeding season when they engage in amplexus and defend nesting territories. The ultimate total length of the species, measured from snout to tail tip, reaches up to 12 centimeters [Li = up to 12 centimeters], making Phaeognathus hubrichti one of the largest lungless salamanders in the southeastern United States. This substantial body size is correlated with its fossorial habits and the need to navigate through tight burrow systems.

Longevity data from recaptures of individually marked animals over two decades suggest that the lifespan of this salamander is remarkably extended for an amphibian of its body size. At the prevailing burrow temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 7,191 days [am = approximately 7,191 days], equivalent to nearly twenty years. This extreme longevity is consistent with the slow pace of life history traits observed in the species, including delayed maturity and low annual reproductive output. Male Red Hills salamanders, in addition to being heavier, also differ in the timing of their sexual development; the snout-vent length at puberty for males has been reported as 7.9 centimeters [Lp = 7.9 centimeters], which is smaller than the 10.1 centimeters [Lp = 10.1 centimeters] required for females to achieve reproductive maturity. This disparity suggests that males may begin breeding at a younger age or smaller size, potentially maximizing their reproductive opportunities within a polygynous mating system where larger territorial males dominate access to females.
